aions_core/agi_existing_models.py: This file acts as a hub that discovers and manages language models already installed on the computer—specifically Mistral-7B, Phi-3 (modified for Korean), and Bielik. It loads each model only when needed, using either llama.cpp for compressed formats or the transformers library for PyTorch models, keeping only one model in memory at a time to save RAM. The file includes Korean syllable compression that reduces text size using patterns, and chunk loading from CBMS (code book memory system) JSON and binary files. When you ask it a question, it picks the best model based on what you're asking about, retrieves relevant chunks from memory, and generates an answer. An ensemble version runs multiple models and picks the best response. The system tracks how fast each query runs and what chunks were used.
aions_core/aions_crla_reformed.py: This file combines cleaned seed data from reformed CBMS with a tournament system (CRLA) for picking the best answer. When you ask a question, it first tries to answer directly from stored facts. If there's no direct answer and the memory system retrieves too many chunks (panic threshold), it generates multiple candidate answers, scores each one using a metric formula, runs them through a tournament, and picks the winner. The winning answer gets saved as a derivation with timestamp and trace showing which candidates were considered. High-confidence direct answers are saved as facts. The system detects when it's overwhelmed with too much information (panic) and switches strategies. The file imports existing modules for memory, CBMS integration, and CRLA scoring, testing the complete workflow.
aions_core/aions_monitoring_dashboard.py: This file is a production-ready monitoring system that watches over an AIONS installation and makes sure everything works. It runs a comprehensive test suite across core, vector search, and hybrid retrieval components, checking that each one responds correctly. The monitoring system tracks how fast queries run, measures success rates, and logs errors. A health check verifies each component is operational. Performance benchmarking runs queries repeatedly and calculates percentiles (95th, 99th) to understand response time distribution. All test results, performance metrics, and error logs get saved to files with timestamps. The system generates a human-readable report showing which components are working, what tests passed or failed, and how the system is performing overall, outputting everything as JSON and text summaries.
aions_core/aions_vector_enhancement.py: This file adds semantic search using LanceDB, a vector database that finds information by meaning rather than exact words. It connects to an existing LanceDB instance used by Kiro (another system in the environment), specifically looking for a table containing knowledge documents. When you search, it scans the database and returns relevant results with similarity scores. The file discovers what tables exist and connects to the main knowledge table. It provides statistics about the database like how many rows are stored. Without the embedding model loaded separately, it does basic limit-scanned retrieval instead of true semantic search, so full text-to-vector search requires additional setup. The connection shows table names and row counts proving it's communicating with the vector database.
aions_core/tools/symbolic_probe.py: This file demonstrates how natural language gets translated into symbolic codes for memory lookups in CBMS. It dynamically loads three helper modules (Esperanto bridge, codebook engine, symbolic index) from the server directory. The demo takes plain-language Polish queries and converts each one to Esperanto as an intermediate step, then encodes the Esperanto into CBMS codes using a codebook. These codes represent concepts in machine-readable way. It then searches the symbolic index for chunks matching those codes and shows which chunk IDs scored highest. The workflow proves that questions like 'I went to the store today' and 'Explain Korean-CBMS segmentation' can be reduced to symbolic patterns that match stored information blocks without needing vector embeddings.
aions_core/tools/test_guardrail.py: This file tests whether the system correctly refuses nonsensical queries and accepts valid ones. It sends HTTP requests to a running server (port 8080) with two test cases: gibberish text that should be rejected, and a legitimate Polish question that should get answered. For each test, it prints the HTTP response status and full JSON reply showing what the server decided. The test demonstrates the guardrail policy—a protective layer that filters out meaningless input to prevent wasting computation on garbage. If the server responds successfully to the good query and refuses the bad one, the guardrail is working. The test can run locally against any AIONS server on 127.0.0.1, validating that input filtering is operational.
control_plane/agents/__init__.py: This docstring-only file explains the agent engine design philosophy: agents are declarations that describe roles within CBMS (code book memory system), not separate execution code. Each agent is a folder containing an agent.json configuration file declaring what it does. The system auto-discovers agents by scanning the agents_lib directory—when you drop a new agent folder there, it's automatically available without touching core code. An agent is essentially a read-only view into the existing skill registry and execution gate with a risk cap. Agents own no logic; they describe how to combine existing skills safely. This plug-and-play architecture means adding new agent roles is configuration, not programming, keeping the system modular and preventing code churn.
control_plane/models.py: This file defines data structures that represent plans and their execution in a control system. A PlanStep contains a task description, the name of the tool that should run it, and arguments for that tool. A Plan collects multiple steps along with an overall intent statement and CBMS context chunks that inform the plan. ExecutionResult records what happened when one step ran: its status, output, error message if it failed, and how long it took in milliseconds. ExecutionState tracks overall progress: which plan is running, what status it's in, which step is currently executing, and the results from all steps so far. Helper functions generate unique IDs for plans and steps using UUID to ensure no collisions.
control_plane/operator/loop.py: This is the operator automation loop that runs continuously to detect and fix system problems. It follows a five-phase cycle: observe (collect system stats), diagnose (identify issues), act (take corrective steps), verify (confirm issues are resolved), and learn (save incident record). The observe phase gathers memory usage, disk usage, failed services, and error log counts using shell skills. Diagnose applies threshold rules—if disk is over 90%, if a service failed, if load average is too high, or if error counts spike. Act recommends fixes or takes automatic action like restarting a service with safeguards like restart cooldowns. Verify re-observes to check whether the fix worked. Learn saves incident records to JSON log, optionally adding LLM commentary in Polish when actions escalate to human review.
scripts/chatgpt_ultimate.py: This script extracts everything stored in ChatGPT Desktop's local cache files and produces a clean inventory. It reads raw LevelDB text dumps and parses them with regex patterns to find user emails, display names, user IDs, message counts, conversation titles, custom GPTs the user created, draft messages, and model access information like GPT-5 availability. Some data is stored as spaced-out text (each letter separated by spaces), so the script reconstructs normal words. It generates two output files: a JSON file with all extracted data organized by category, and a markdown report showing conversation history, model access levels, and custom GPT list. The script handles encoding issues and malformed data gracefully, keeping everything readable.
scripts/demo_papiery.py: This demo script shows how to use CBMS blocks to manage personal tasks and reminders like a digital secretary. It loads the skill registry which discovers all available CBMS blocks, then adds sample papers (tasks) with titles, deadlines, and priority levels. The secretary then lists all stored papers, finds papers due soon (within 7 days), and sends a system notification reminding the user of urgent items. The script also searches for papers matching a keyword. Finally, it demonstrates how the skill registry's search function picks the right CBMS block for a question by returning the best match. All task data lives in local JSON files within your CBMS directory, not in a remote database. The demo proves CBMS blocks can replace apps for task management.
scripts/test_llm_adapter.py: This test verifies that the Polish language model (Bielik via Ollama) answers correctly and uses injected context. It defines test questions with expected keywords that prove context was used: 'Who am I?' should mention the operator's name from operator_profile.json, and 'What is CBMS?' should reference the chunked memory system with words like 'chunks' or 'memory'. The test runs each question, checks if the response contains Polish language indicators (Polish characters and common words), then checks if expected context keywords appear. If the model responds in Polish AND uses provided context, the test passes. The script handles Ollama server availability gracefully, reporting whether the model endpoint is reachable and which models are loaded.
scripts/validate_aions_tools.py: This script quickly validates that MCP (Model Context Protocol) tool functions work after code changes. It imports tool implementations from the server module and runs quick tests: search for Python files, search in specific folders, check system health, search the code book memory, retrieve facts from long-term memory, check git status, list WSL distributions, list Docker containers, check project scan status, check conversation status, list MCP servers, and check thinking process status. Each tool should return a response with status='ok' or status='completed'. The script counts how many tests passed and reports totals. This is a smoke test confirming the server can execute its tools—useful after changes to ensure nothing broke.
server/app.py: This is the main REST API server that manages a knowledge base with sessions, search, and document storage. Built with FastAPI, it listens for HTTP requests to add documents to a session, search for relevant documents, and manage sessions. Sessions are like workspaces—each one has its own collection of documents. The API provides endpoints to add context batches (text plus metadata), search using a query with optional filters, list all sessions with statistics, get details about one session, dump all documents from a session, prune expired documents, and view a dashboard summary. The server connects to a vector store (ChromaDB) that actually holds the data. CORS is enabled so clients from any origin can connect. Optional control plane routes can be added if available.
server/store_http.py: This file implements the vector storage backend using ChromaDB with two connection modes: HTTP (connecting to a remote server) or embedded (local storage). It tries first to connect via HTTP to a ChromaDB server on 127.0.0.1:8000, falling back to embedded mode if the server is down. Collections are created per session, keeping documents and their metadata organized. When you search, it converts Chroma's distance scores to similarity scores (0 to 1) accounting for the actual distance metric used (L2, cosine, inner product). It handles keyword boosting to increase scores for documents matching all query words. The store tracks which mode it's using and logs degraded-to-embedded failures to a runtime log. It can reconnect to HTTP mode later if the server comes back online.
This file runs a production-ready system that compresses Polish and technical words into syllable patterns for faster neural processing. It loads a special version of the Phi-3 language model that has been tuned to recognize Korean linguistic patterns, then takes text input and breaks it into syllables that have meaning, assigns each a color code and semantic label, and processes them through the neural network to produce an understanding of what the text means with an efficiency score. The core pieces are: a dictionary of known syllable patterns and their meanings, a function that splits words into these patterns by checking the longest matches first, a function that maps each syllable to a data block with Korean mapping, and a final response generator that combines all the semantic pieces. Input is Polish or English text phrases; output is a JSON file containing the original text, syllable breakdown, compression ratios, semantic meanings, and overall system efficiency percentages. It talks to PyTorch for neural operations, reads safetensors model weights from disk, and writes the final production results to a JSON output file. Someone working with this would use it to speed up language processing for a language model by compressing complex words into their semantic building blocks.
aions_core/agi_evolution.py: This file manages automatic self-improvement for an artificial intelligence system by tracking what it does well and what it struggles with, then proposing and testing changes to make it better. It keeps a history of performance on eight different skills—like how fast it responds, how accurate its confidence predictions are, and how well it learns from examples—and when performance drops, it suggests improvement strategies such as doing deeper reasoning, trying new ideas, or consolidating what it already knows. The main pieces are: data structures for storing performance measurements over time, a list of predefined improvement strategies with success rates, functions to analyze performance from interaction data, functions to select which strategies to apply based on weaknesses, and a history log of all evolution attempts. Input is feedback about how well the system performed on tasks; output is improvement plans, updated metrics, strategy success rates, and a readiness assessment (Initial/Developing/Competent/Advanced/Expert). It interacts with AGI core and learning modules to apply changes, reads and writes configuration files in JSON format, and keeps all state in memory with the ability to save it. Users would think of this as the part of the system that makes the AI get smarter by learning from its mistakes.
aions_core/agi_neural_backprop.py: This file implements a neural network system that can learn from feedback by tracking how errors flow backward through its layers, allowing it to adjust its thinking process. It combines several neural building blocks: an embedder that converts text chunks into learnable vectors, a multi-hop reasoning graph that combines knowledge to answer questions with attention to which knowledge matters most, and differentiable memory that can read and write using soft addressing so gradients can flow through everything. The main components are embedding layers for tokenizing and positioning, transformer encoders for processing, a multi-step reasoning network with gated recurrent units, memory read/write controllers with attention mechanisms, and loss functions for confidence, knowledge consistency, and continuous improvement. Input is a query string and knowledge chunks as dictionaries; output is a response embedding, confidence score, and the reasoning path it took. The system runs on GPU if available (CUDA), saves checkpoints to disk, and analyzes gradient flow to detect learning problems like vanishing or exploding gradients. Someone using this would see it as the trainable thinking engine that improves by comparing its outputs against ground truth feedback.
aions_core/api.py: This file starts a web server that listens for incoming questions and routes them to the unified AIONS core system for processing. It uses FastAPI to create HTTP endpoints and forces all transformer libraries to work offline from cached models to avoid network issues. The main pieces are: startup code that initializes the AIONS v2 system with all Phase 4 components enabled (vector search, hybrid logic, agent system, styling, monitoring), a health check that runs on startup to verify everything loads correctly, and three HTTP endpoints—one to answer queries, one to check status, and one to report root health. Input comes as JSON with a query string field; output is a JSON response from the processing system, or an error message if something fails. It imports the unified_core module from the local directory and also tries to handle import errors by appending to sys.path, talks to all AIONS subsystems through the aions object, and returns HTTP status codes (503 for not ready, 500 for runtime error, 200 for success). A developer would use this as the entry point to talk to the AIONS system from external clients over HTTP.
aions_core/server/stylist.py: This file cleans up the formatting and whitespace in text answers without changing the actual facts or content. It normalizes spaces and newlines, fixes capitalization if needed, ensures bracketed source citations are on separate paragraphs, and then verifies that nothing important was lost by checking that all numbers, bracketed blocks, and structured elements are still present in the same quantities. The main pieces are: a whitespace normalization function that collapses multiple spaces and lines but preserves line breaks and structure, safety pattern checking that collects all numbers and bracketed sections before and after styling to compare them, and a main style_pass function that runs the cleanup and reports whether changes were made or if something went wrong. Input is a string answer that might have messy spacing or inconsistent formatting; output is the cleaned text plus a boolean saying if changes were applied plus a message code explaining success or failure. It uses regular expressions to find and verify patterns, doesn't call external systems, and is designed to be lightweight. Someone would use this when they have a wordy response that needs to look professional but the actual information must stay exactly correct.
aions_core/server/ts_symbols.py: This file reads source code files in multiple programming languages, extracts all the function and class definitions and their relationships, and packages them as knowledge chunks ready to store in a searchable memory system. It uses tree-sitter, a parser that builds an abstract syntax tree from code, to walk through the code structure, identify named definitions and their line numbers, collect what other code each one calls or imports, and compute a hash of each body so you can tell later if something changed without re-parsing everything. The main pieces are: a Symbol class storing metadata about each code element with its name path, kind (function/class/method/etc), line range, signature, docstring, and soft references to other code; a SymbolIndex class that loads a file, parses it, and builds a queryable dictionary of symbols; and scanning functions that process entire directories. Input is a source file path in any supported language (Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Rust, Java, C++, etc); output is an outline showing all symbols in the file with their kind and line numbers, or full chunk candidates that include docstrings and body code formatted for storage. It talks to tree-sitter-language-pack to parse code, reads source files from disk, and outputs JSON files with chunk candidates. Someone would use this to convert their codebase into a searchable knowledge base where the system can look up what any function does.
aions_core/smart_cbms.py: This file speeds up question answering by trying to find the answer instantly in a cached knowledge system first, and only asking a larger language model if the cache doesn't have enough information. It measures how fast each stage takes, composes a very short prompt if it must call the language model, and combines the instant answer with the model's response into a final answer. The main pieces are: a CBMS memory object that instantly thinks through a question and returns matching knowledge chunks, logic to decide whether the cached answer is good enough or whether Bielik (a local language model) needs to be called, code that measures response time at each stage, a request formatter that sends only keywords to Bielik to keep the prompt tiny, and error handling if Bielik times out or is unavailable. Input is a natural language question; output is a string answer with timing information and a source attribution saying whether it came from CBMS cache, Bielik model, or both. It calls the CBMS memory system for instant retrieval, makes HTTP POST requests to a local LLM server on port 11434, tries to timeout quickly if the model is slow, and has two demo modes: a speed test and an interactive chat. Someone would use this when they want answers in under 100 milliseconds and are willing to trust cached knowledge for common questions.
This file scans all the knowledge chunks stored on disk, updates an index file that lists what chunks exist and what topics they cover, so the knowledge system can quickly find relevant information later without loading every file. It reads all JSON chunk files from disk, extracts the chunk ID and topic from each, and rebuilds two maps: one that lists every chunk with its topic and size, and another that groups chunk IDs by topic. The main pieces are: logic to find the manifest file and initialize it if it doesn't exist, a loop that reads every JSON chunk file and extracts its metadata, updating code that adds each chunk to both the ID index and the topic-grouped map, and final save code that writes the rebuilt manifest back to disk. Input is disk access to read all chunk JSON files; output is a manifest.json file containing version number, creation timestamp, a flat index mapping chunk IDs to concept/size/file, a concept map grouping chunk IDs by their topic, and a total chunk count. It interacts with the filesystem by reading chunks and writing the manifest, and reports progress every 200 chunks processed. Someone would run this when they add new chunks to the knowledge base or suspect the index is out of sync with what's actually on disk.
control_plane/node_registry.py: This file maintains a list of available worker machines in the system, tracking what each one can do, whether it is healthy, how busy it is, and what permissions it has, so tasks can be routed to the best machine for each job. It keeps this registry in memory with optional saving to disk as JSON, loads the registry at startup from a saved file if it exists, and creates a default local development node if the registry is empty. The main pieces are: a NodeRecord dataclass holding one machine's ID, hostname, capabilities list, memory amount, available tools, health status, load percentage, and permissions; functions to register new machines or update existing ones; functions to list all nodes or find the best node for a specific task; and persistence code that reads from and writes to a JSON state file. Input is registration calls with machine details or heartbeat updates with current health and load; output is NodeRecord objects and query results showing which machines are available and healthy. It reads and writes to a JSON file in a configurable state directory, detects whether it is running on Windows or Linux to set default capabilities, and implements staleness checking so stale heartbeats can be ignored. Someone would use this as the component that decides which backend machine should handle a particular request.
control_plane/skills/planner.py: This file decides how to execute a task by checking if there is a cached recipe for that kind of task, and if not, gathering available skills that can help solve it and filtering out any that cannot run right now. It is very short and delegates the hard work to recipe lookup and world state checking. The main pieces are: a call to find a matching recipe based on the task intent, a search through available skills if no recipe exists, per-skill checking of whether world conditions block that skill from running, and return of either a recipe to replay or a list of candidate skills for a stronger model to compose into a plan. Input is a registry of available skills and an intent string describing what the user wants; output is a JSON structure containing either a recipe ID and steps, or a list of candidate skills with information about which ones are currently blocked by world state. It calls recipe lookup and world state matching functions, and is designed to be called by a planner orchestrator that has access to the skill registry and current environment state. Someone would think of this as the part that finds the right tools or cached procedures for a job.
mcpServers/VS_CODE_MCP_CODEX/src/filesys: This file creates and maintains an index of all files and directories in specified folders, allowing very fast file searches without scanning disk every time. It builds a JSON index file containing every file and folder path found, with metadata like size and modification time, then answers search queries by looking in the index instead of walking the directory tree. The main pieces are: configuration for which root directories to index and which folders to skip (like .git and node_modules), index generation code that walks the file tree and creates entry dictionaries for each file and folder, search functions that match query text against stored paths and rank them by how well they match, and staleness checking so the index is refreshed automatically if it gets too old. Input is a search query string or file extension filter and a max results limit; output is a list of matching file paths ranked by score. It reads the filesystem to build the index, stores the index as a JSON file with customizable location and refresh interval, and compares queries against file names, paths, and relative paths with different scoring for exact match, prefix, substring, or path match. Someone would use this to search for files by name or pattern much faster than the operating system file search.
scripts/aions_python.sh: This file is a bash launcher that finds and uses the correct Python virtual environment from configuration, so all AIONS scripts use exactly the same Python version and installed packages regardless of where they are called from. It reads configuration from a file that specifies which Python version and which venv directory to use, verifies that the venv exists and has the right Python version, creates the venv if needed, and then either shows the path to Python or executes a command with that Python. The main pieces are: config file reading that parses key-value pairs and extracts the Python version and venv path, version verification that actually runs Python to check it matches expectations, venv setup code that creates a fresh venv and installs dependencies from a requirements file, and mode handling to support resolve-only, ensure-venv-only, or run-command modes. Input is command-line arguments like --resolve to print the path, --ensure-venv to set up if needed, or Python arguments to execute; output is either the Python executable path printed to stdout or execution of a Python command with that interpreter. It reads the python.env configuration file from the .aions directory, checks Linux and Windows paths depending on platform, and looks for a fallback config if the main one is not found. Someone would use this as a safe wrapper ensuring that when they run AIONS Python scripts in any shell context, they always get the environment they expect.
scripts/ingest_treasures_tier2.py: This file reads a catalog of important files and folders stored elsewhere on disk, converts that catalog into searchable summaries, and stores those summaries in a vector database so the system can later find relevant treasure data by searching for keywords. It does not copy the actual files—just their metadata, paths, types, and descriptions. The main pieces are: a catalog loader that reads from a catalog JSON file, formatting code that turns each catalog entry into a readable summary with path, type, status, and file counts, metadata builders that attach proper tags and timestamps, and vector store code that saves the summaries to Chroma database collections. Input is a JSON catalog file containing treasure entries with paths, types, file counts, and status; output is the summaries stored in two Chroma collections: one for system operators and one for the user's knowledge base. It checks the Chroma version to ensure it is the 0.5.x format compatible with the production database, reads and parses the catalog JSON, interacts with the VectorStore class to perform the actual storage, and can run in dry-run mode to show what would be stored. Someone would run this after updating a catalog to make that metadata searchable in the knowledge system.
scripts/verify_tier1_chroma.py: This file runs tests to check that the vector database was set up correctly and contains expected data, doing a few searches to verify that the right information can be found. It does not modify anything, just reports on the state of the database. The main pieces are: code that initializes a connection to the Chroma database, functions that perform test searches on stored data like looking for operator profiles or CBMS keywords, code that retrieves statistics about how many documents are in each collection, and verification logic that checks whether the minimum expected numbers are met. Input is environment variables for the Chroma path if set, otherwise defaults to a standard location; output is a JSON report showing the Chroma path, list of available sessions/collections, sample search results from operator and main knowledge bases, statistics on document counts per collection, and a pass/fail result code. It calls VectorStore to connect to the database, performs actual search queries to verify data was ingested, checks that at least 2 documents are in the operator collection and 10 in the main collection and that searches return at least one result each, and reports all findings as JSON. Someone would run this after ingesting data to confirm that everything was stored correctly and can be retrieved.
server/__init__.py: This is a Python package marker file indicating that the server directory is a Python package and can be imported.
